questions.prompt: What does the “Systemic Safety” strategy in the Disaster Risk Equation primarily aim to achieve?
options: Improve a specific model’s ability to withstand external hazards
Identify and avoid hazards through real-time monitoring
Reduce the likelihood of conflict and overall systemic risks in the environment
Align an agent’s goals with human values
questions.solution: AI Risk Part 3 [34:02-34:55] - We can look at the risk equation as a "systemic” safety, which in turn can generally reduce the risks.

questions.prompt: In the context of “Deceptive Alignment,” what is the primary concern regarding model behavior?
options: The model appears to follow safety guidelines during training but pursues different goals after deployment
The model cannot understand human language due to environmental differences
The model accidentally deletes critical memory during deployment
The model’s safeguards are easily bypassed by simple user prompts
questions.solution: AI Risk Part 4 [23:34-24:23] - Deceptive alignment is shown by the example as the model appearing to grab the ball/asnwer a specific way but later doesn’t.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, why is “proxy gaming” considered a failure mode in AI systems?
options: Agents over-optimize fault metrics, producing outcomes misaligned with true human values
AI systems consume excessive computational resources unnecessarily
AI systems are used to cheat in video games
It results from hardware failure during large-scale simulations
questions.solution: AI Risk Part 4 [20:26-22:17] - Future artificial agents could over-optimize and game faulty proxies, which could mean systems aggressively pursue goals and create a world that is distinct from what humans value.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, why might AI systems develop an “instrumental incentive” to seek power?
options: They are explicitly programmed to dominate humans
Power and resources help them pursue their goals more effectively
It is a biological byproduct of the neural network design
They imitate human power-seeking behavior from training data
questions.solution: AI Risk Part 4 [9:51-11:50] - By default, suitably strategic and intelligent agents, engaging in suitable types of planning, will have instrumental incentives to gain and maintain various types of power, since this power will help them pursue their objectives more effectively.

questions.prompt: What does the term “Treacherous Turns” refer to in AI safety?
options: Failures caused by biased training data
A system behaving differently once sufficiently capable
Intentional misuse of AI by malicious humans
Over-optimization of proxy objectives
questions.solution: AI Risk Part 4 [22:18-23:34] - AI could behave differently once it has the ability to do so.

questions.prompt: According to the “Swiss cheese model”, which statement best describes effective safety design?
options: Rely on a single, highly robust safety mechanism
Implement safety measures randomly across the system
Use multiple layers of defense so that individual weaknesses are compensated by others
Eliminate safety measures if the AI system is well-designed
questions.solution: AI Risk Part 3 [8:18-10:48] - The Swiss Cheese model shows how technical factors can improve organizational safety. Multiple layers of defense compensate for each other’s individual weaknesses, leading to a low overall level of risk.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, what are the potential “double-edged sword” risks associated with AI in military applications? (Select all that apply.)

Complete elimination of the need for human strategic decision-making
Lowering the barriers to large-scale violence
Autonomous retaliation systems increasing the risk of rapid escalation

Reducing the severity of inherent model vulnerabilities
questions.solution: AI Risk Part 3 [29:45-34:02] - Each component has one way to mitigate/reduce it. Vulnerability: Robustness; Hazard Exposure: Monitoring; Hazard: Alignment.

questions.prompt: Match the unlearning method to their corresponding concept.

rows: i) Unlearned model and retrained model are distributionally close
ii) The forget set is clearly defined
iii) The forget set is not clearly defined
iv) Unlearned model and retrained model are distributionally identical

questions.solution: Answers are found throughout the Unlearning and Approximate Unlearning lectures - ● Exact Unlearning - Unlearned model & retrained model to be distributionally identical. ● Unlearning via Differential Privacy - Unlearned model & retrained model to be distributionally close. ● Example Unlearning - Train, retain, and forget sets are often clearly defined. ● Concept Unlearning - Train, retain, or forget sets are poorly specified or just not ● specified at all.

options: KL Divergence
Direct Preference Optimization
Gradient Ascent

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, what is “Representation Engineering”?
options: A bottom-up approach focusing on individual neurons.
Modifying representation vectors to control model traits.
A method for increasing the parameter count of a model.
Re-labeling all data points in a dataset to fix biases.
questions.solution: Evaluation of Unlearning and Graph Unlearning Part 1 [30:35-33:10] - Modify the representation vectors to modify the model outputs.

questions.prompt: In the context of the SISA framework, how does the system minimize the cost of retraining when a data point must be unlearned?
options: By using gradient ascent on only the affected data points.
By applying a differential privacy constraint to the aggregation layer.
By flipping the labels of the forget set and performing few-shot.
By retraining only the constituent model whose shards contain the point to be unlearned.
questions.solution: Unlearning [25:00-29:43] - SISA training: data is divided in shards, which are themselves divided into slices. One constituent model is trained on each shard by presenting it with incrementally many slices and saving its parameters before the training set is augmented with a new slice. When data needs to be unlearned, only one of the constituent models whose shards contain the point to be unlearned needs to be retrained — retraining can start from the last parameter values saved before including the slice containing the data point to be unlearned.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, why is unlearning fundamental facts like “the sun rises every day” considered more difficult than unlearning infrequent textual occurrences, such as car accidents?
options: Fundamental knowledge is deeply embedded in the model’s implicit knowledge graph.
Fundamental facts are typically protected by guardrails.
Models are primarily trained on Wikipedia, which contains these facts.
Differential privacy guarantees fall off more quickly for fundamental facts.
questions.solution: Evaluation of Unlearning and Graph Unlearning Part 1 [25:25-27:16] - A piece of knowledge can be so embedded in the model’s implicit knowledge graph that it cannot be unlearned without introducing contradictions and harming the model’s utility.

questions.prompt: Which unlearning evaluation metric focuses on whether the unlearning process negatively affects the model’s performance on the “retrain data” or unrelated tasks?

Model Utility

questions.solution: Approximate Unlearning [25:55-27:35] - Model utility: Do we harm performance on the retain data or orthogonal tasks?

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the correct setting for contrastive learning? (Select all that apply.)
options: Irrespective of the sentences, minimise the distance between their embeddings.
Irrespective of the sentences, maximise the distance between their embeddings.
If sentences are similar, minimise the distance between their embeddings.
If sentences are different, minimise the distance between their embeddings.
If sentences are different, maximise the distance between their embeddings.
If sentences are different, minimise the distance between their embeddings
questions.solution: Contrastive learning trains models by pulling similar items together and pushing dissimilar items apart. It achieves this by minimizing the embedding distance for similar sentences and maximizing the distance for different ones.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, why would standard cryptographic solutions be unsuitable for AI model privacy? (Select all that apply.)

questions.prompt: In the randomized response algorithm presented in the lecture, what is the minimum probability that the truthful answer is revealed?
questions.solution: Data Privacy [21:25-24:12] - ε > 0 means that the truth will be revealed with a probability of e^ε / (1 + e^ε) > 50%.

questions.prompt: To maximize utility, how should the privacy parameter ε be adjusted?
options: ε should be maximum for privacy, ε should be minimum for utility
ε should be minimum for privacy, ε should be minimum for utility
ε should be maximum for privacy, ε should be maximum for utility
ε should be minimum for privacy, ε should be maximum for utility
ε is unrelated
questions.solution: Data Privacy [1:00:00 - 1:01:20] - If ε is large, x_i and z_i are easier to distinguish, which increases utility, and vice versa. ε controls the privacy-utility tradeoff.

questions.prompt: An organization surveys 100 people and asks whether they voted for a certain party. To protect respondents' privacy, the organization uses the randomized response technique with ε = 0.5. Out of 100 respondents, 60 reported “Yes” and 40 reported “No.” Estimate the true number of people whose actual answer was “Yes”. Round to the nearest whole number.
questions.solution: Data Privacy - with ε = 0.5 a response is truthful with probability e^ε / (1 + e^ε) ≈ 0.6225, so the estimate is (60 − 100·(1 − 0.6225)) / (2·0.6225 − 1) ≈ 91.

questions.prompt: Which trust scenario correctly describes the differential privacy model?
options: Trust the curator; Trust the world
Do not trust the curator; Trust the world
Trust the curator; Do not trust the world
Do not trust the curator; Do not trust the world
questions.solution: Data Privacy [1:06:06-1:11:00] - In differential privacy, surveyors trust the curator to give their information to them but want their information to be privatized when the computed function is released to the world.

questions.prompt: In the Laplace Mechanism, how is the sensitivity (Δ) defined for a function f?
options: The average difference between f(X) and f(X') for all neighbouring X and X'.
The maximum absolute difference between f(X) and f(X') for any two neighboring X and X'.
The standard deviation of the function f.
The minimum difference between f(X) and f(X') for any two neighboring X and X'.
questions.solution: Differential Privacy [21:30-22:34] - Sensitivity (Δ) in the Laplace mechanism measures how sensitive a function f is to a single input change. It is the maximum absolute difference |f(X) − f(X')| over all neighboring datasets X and X' that differ by one element.

questions.prompt: According to Cynthia Dwork's definition of ε-differential privacy, for all neighbouring datasets X and X', the probability that a mechanism M on X generates an output in subset S divided by the probability that a mechanism M on X' generates an output in subset S is at most:
options: e^ε
ε
ε^e
questions.solution: Differential Privacy [9:57-15:02] - A mechanism M is said to be ε-differential private if Pr(M(X) ∈ S) / Pr(M(X') ∈ S) ≤ e^ε.

questions.prompt: What property of neighboring data sets X and X' is used to prove the privacy guarantee of Randomized Response?
options: They have zero correlation.
They differ by 99% of the elements in the set.
They are disjoint sets.
They differ by only one element.
questions.solution: Data Privacy [24:29-25:58] - X and X' are two datasets where X = X' for all i ∈ {1 ... (n − 1)}, meaning they differ by only one element of index i = n.

questions.prompt: For a fixed ε, if a function being computed is highly sensitive (large Δ), how does it affect the noise added to the Laplace mechanism?
options: Less noise is added.
More noise is added.
The noise remains unchanged.
Noise is irrelevant.
questions.solution: Differential Privacy [27:14-31:00] - The more sensitive the function, the more noise should be added.

questions.prompt: Comparing the Laplace mechanism and randomized response, how does the required number of respondents n differ to achieve the same privacy–utility trade-off?
options: The Laplace mechanism requires quadratically more people.
The Laplace mechanism requires quadratically fewer people.
Both require the same number of people.
The number of people to survey does not matter.
questions.solution: Differential Privacy [50:18-53:02] - If you trust the curator, then you would have to survey a quadratically lesser number of people to achieve the same privacy-utility tradeoff using the Laplace mechanism than not trusting the curator.

questions.prompt: In Approximate Differential Privacy, what does δ represent?
options: The strict upper bound of the probability of the mechanism M.
The estimated noise added to the Laplace Mechanism.
The average difference between all the data points in the datasets X and X'.
A leeway for small-probability events where ε-differential privacy may fail.
questions.solution: Approximate Differential Privacy [6:50-9:26] - δ is a small leeway for low probability events where ε-differential privacy property may not hold true.

questions.prompt: Compared to the Laplacian mechanism, how does the Gaussian mechanism scale the amount of noise added when releasing D different outputs?
options: It adds noise linearly proportional to D.
It adds noise proportional to the square root of D.
It adds noise exponentially proportional to D.
It adds the same amount of noise.
questions.solution: Approximate Differential Privacy [18:00-20:58] - The Guassian Mechanism requires quadratically less amount of noise to become in terms of number of output that you're releasing.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are properties of Approximate Differential Privacy? (Select all that apply.)
options: It satisfies the property of post-processing, meaning any data-independent computation applied to the output will not make it less (ε, δ)-differentially private.
It guarantees privacy even when δ is significantly larger than 1/n (where n is the number of individuals in a dataset).
It satisfies composition, meaning if you have k mechanisms that are all (ε, δ)-differentially private, then the combined mechanism is (kε, kδ)-differentially private.
It guarantees that the output distributions of the algorithm are completely identical for any two neighboring datasets.
questions.solution: Approximate Differential Privacy [23:40-34:53] - Approximate differential privacy has two properties: post-processing and composition.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, what is the primary advantage of using the Gaussian Mechanism?
options: Zero chance of privacy leakage.
Faster computational time for calculating probabilities.
Better utility due to adding quadratically less noise.
Eliminates the need for a trusted curator.
questions.solution: Approximate Differential Privacy [14:45-22:55] - Gaussian mechanism gains better utility with quadratically less amount of noise.

questions.prompt: There are three buyers whose valuations are 15, 20, and 135, respectively. What is the absolute difference in revenue when the price of a digital good changes from 14 to 18? (Round your answer to the nearest whole number.)
questions.solution: Exponential Mechanism - revenue at price 14 is 3 × 14 = 42 and at price 18 is 2 × 18 = 36 (the buyer valuing it at 15 no longer buys), so the difference is 6.

questions.prompt: How does the Exponential Mechanism select a price h ∈ H?
options: With probability proportional to the inverse of the price.
With probability proportional to e^(ε/(2δ) · S(x, h)).
With probability proportional to e^(δ/(2ε) · S(x, h)).
Uniformly at random from all prices below the maximum valuation.
questions.solution: Exponential Mechanism [14:11-15:00] - Select h ∈ H with probability proportional to e^(ε/(2δ) · S(x, h)).

questions.prompt: What privacy guarantee does the Exponential Mechanism provide for buyers' valuations?
options: (ε, δ)-Differential Privacy
ε-Differential Privacy
K-Anonymity
Concentrated Differential Privacy
questions.solution: Exponential Mechanism [15:53-18:15] - Exponential mechanism is Epsilon differentially private for the given valuations.

questions.prompt: What is the utility guarantee provided by the Exponential Mechanism?
options: It guarantees the absolute highest possible revenue every time.
It does not guarantee positive revenue every time.
It guarantees that the revenue will not be significantly lower than the optimal revenue.
The guarantee will exactly match the median valuation.
questions.solution: Exponential Mechanism [18:15-22:35] - It guarantees that the revenue will not be significantly lower than the optimal revenue.

questions.prompt: In Statistical Parity, for a protected group C and a classifier M, what is the parity value for an ideal classifier?
questions.solution: Fairness in Machine Learning [47:03-50:41] - An ideal classifier has a parity equal to 0.

questions.prompt: According to the data comparing White and African American defendants in risk assessments, which of the following statements are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: White defendants were labeled lower risk yet did re-offend at a higher rate than African American defendants.
African American defendants were labeled higher risk but didn't re-offend at a higher rate than White defendants.
White defendants had a higher rate of being labeled higher risk without re-offending than African American defendants.
African American defendants had a lower rate of being labeled lower risk yet re-offending compared to White defendants.
questions.solution: Fairness in Machine Learning [19:42-21:38] - According to the table: ● A higher percentage of African Americans were labelled as higher risk but didn’t re-offend ● A higher percentage of White people were labelled as low risk but did re-offend. ● A lower percentage of African Americans were labelled as lower risk yet re-offended compared to White people.

questions.prompt: Based on the analysis of biases in word embeddings from Wikipedia and Social Media, which of the following professions was associated with sexist prejudice towards men?
options: Nurse
Teacher
Pharmacist
Cameraman
questions.solution: Fairness in Machine Learning [24:44-28:10] - According to the lecture, “Cameraman” is a profession that is associated with sexist prejudice towards men.

questions.prompt: The goal of Fair PCA is to find a PCA solution U = [U_A, U_B] such that the reconstruction losses of groups A and B (where A is the protected group) are:

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes Pixel Attribution Methods?

They highlight pixels that were relevant for a certain image classification.

questions.prompt: Which of the following pixel attribution methods involve manipulating parts of an image to generate explanations?
options: Gradient-based methods
Occlusion-based methods
Mechanical methods
Top-down methods
questions.solution: Interpretability - I [6:33-7:25] - Occlusion- or perturbation-based: Methods like SHAP and LIME manipulate parts of the image to generate explanations (model-agnostic).

questions.prompt: What should happen to a saliency map if a model that genuinely captures higher-level class concepts has its layers randomized?
options: The map should invert its colors.
The map should remain identical.
The map should change significantly.
The map should become a blank image.
questions.solution: Interpretability - I [20:11-22:28] - If a model captures higher-level class concepts, then saliency maps should change as the model is being randomized.

questions.prompt: How can we validate the explanations given by LIME? (Select all that apply.)
options: By using prior knowledge.
By randomizing the model’s layers.
By using human annotators.
By applying adversarial perturbations.
questions.solution: Interpretability - I [25:10-27:03] - Using prior knowledge, we can validate the explanations. Human annotation can be used to decide whether the model's explanations are correct.

questions.prompt: Which of the following interpretability approaches involves locating information in a model without fully understanding how it is processed?

Feature-based visualization
Game-theoretic approach
questions.solution: Interpretability - II [9:57-11:58] - Top-down locates information in a model without full understanding of how it is processed

options: To inject hidden trojans into public datasets during training.
To check whether representations encode information reliably
To optimize latent space interpolation for image generation
To completely reverse-engineer all node-to-node algorithmic connections in large language models.
questions.solution: Interpretability - II [13:57-16:33] - Probing loosely refers to a class of methodologies in interpretability to check whether representations encode information reliably for some specific task.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, which of the following are Attack Vectors? (Select all that apply.)
options: API keys
Public Datasets
HuggingFace models
A downloadable execution file
questions.solution: Interpretability - II [20:32-21:23] - Public datasets and model sharing libraries are some examples of attack vectors.

questions.prompt: Consider the following equation for LIME: ξ(x) = argmin over g ∈ G of  L(f, g, π_x) + Ω(g). What do the components L and Ω(g) represent?
options: L measures how unfaithful the explanation model g is in approximating f locally (weighted by π_x), while Ω(g) measures the complexity/interpretability penalty of the explanation model.
L represents the global accuracy of the black-box model f, and Ω(g) represents the total number of convolutional layers.
L is the adversarial perturbation budget, and Ω(g) is the learning rate of the surrogate model.
L calculates the exact Shapley values, and Ω(g) computes the gradient with respect to input pixels.
questions.solution: Interpretability - I [32:03-34:57] - In LIME's objective function, L quantifies how poorly the simple explanation model g approximates the complex black-box model f within the local neighborhood defined by π_x, while Ω(g) penalizes model complexity to ensure the resulting explanation remains simple and interpretable for humans.

questions.prompt: What is the primary goal of Neural Cleanse when detecting Trojans in neural networks?
options: To fine-tune the model using a 0.05% poisoned dataset
To reverse-engineer potential triggers
To prune the entire first-layer weights of a classifier
To train a neural network using high-dimensional pooling layers
questions.solution: Interpretability - II [26:57-31:36] - If we know the general form of the attack, we can reverse-engineer the Trojan by searching for a trigger and target label.

questions.prompt: How does top-down interpretability differ from mechanistic interpretability?
options: Top-down focuses on algorithmic node-to-node connections, whereas mechanistic looks at global activity of populations of neurons.
Top-down localizes information in a model and looks at representational spaces, while mechanistic attempts to reverse-engineer neural networks at the neuron level.
Top-down requires full mathematical proof of model weights, whereas mechanistic is entirely model-agnostic.
Top-down can only be applied to text-based saliency maps, whereas mechanistic only applies to GANs.
questions.solution: Interpretability - II [6:27-11:58] - Mechanistic: Reverse-engineer neural Networks; Top-Down: Locate information in a model without full understanding of how it is processed.

questions.prompt: What game-theoretic concept does SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) explain about the output of any machine learning model?
options: Nash Equilibrium
Pareto Optimality
Shapley Values
Minimax Theorem
questions.solution: Interpretability - I [35:20-39:39] - Connects optimal credit allocation with local explanations using the classic Shapley values from game theory and their related extensions.

questions.prompt: Regarding LIME and SHAP, which of the following statements are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: They generate global explanations that apply uniformly across the entire dataset.

Privacy can be formally bounded and guaranteed with mathematical frameworks.
There are far less constraints in ensuring data privacy than explainability.
questions.solution: AI Policies, Regulations, AGI - Part 2 [14:20-14:50] - Mathematical frameworks like differential privacy or cryptography provide proven security guarantees, explainability is black-box and remains harder to formally bound.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, as AI systems become autonomous agents capable of performing complex tasks independently, what is the main trade-off that occurs regarding human decision-making.

Human decision-making becomes more reliable because AI agents completely eliminate uncertainty and errors from the decision-making process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are privacy-preserving training techniques? (Select all that apply.)

questions.prompt: In structured AI governance, what is defines a “co-regulation” model from from strict-regulation or self-regulation?

questions.solution: AI Policies, Regulations, AGI - Part 2 [49:10-51:06] - Co-regulation combines industry expertise in defining baseline standards with government authorization to enforce them across the industry.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, if copyrighted data is found inside a large AI model and must be removed, what is a major technical challenge?

Moving model inference to run on CPUs/Edge devices instead of GPUs.

questions.solution: AI Policies, AGI with Prof. David Krueger - Part 2 [27:19-28:08] - Optimizing persuasiveness gives AI systems leverage to manipulate human behaviour and intention, essentially using human beings as a means to an end.

questions.prompt: Why is it better to have upstream regulation for companies developing AI systems and hardware than having downstream regulation on the people using the AI systems?

options: Text processing requires higher computational memory.

Language models cannot represent abstract reasoning.
Excluding human modalities creates a gap in real-world understanding.
questions.solution: AI Policies, AGI with Prof. David Krueger - Part 2 [13:18-13:37] - Multimodality is a crucial component for AGI, as without it, it creates a qualitative cognitive deficit.

questions.prompt: In the context of data privacy, which right requires companies to delete user data when requested?

Right to be forgotten

questions.prompt: Under the EU AI Act, which application category is classified as an 'unacceptable risk'? (Select all that apply.)
options: Social Scoring Systems
Critical Infrastructure Management
Law Enforcement
Cognitive Behavioural Manipulation
questions.solution: AI Governance [25:22-26:56] - According to the EU AI Act, social scoring and cognitive behavioural manipulation are unacceptable risks.

questions.prompt: When a system like an email spam server filters out malicious messages in the background without requiring user intervention, which type of threat mitigation is it demonstrating?
options: Educating and training users
Providing interface-level threat warnings
Silently eliminating the threat
Enforcing legal regulations
questions.solution: AI Governance [4:41-8:17] - Spam servers operate behind the scenes to remove unwanted or dangerous emails automatically.

questions.prompt: What specific transparency requirement does the EU AI Act impose on deepfakes or generated media?
options: They must be exclusively hosted on European-based servers.
They must be clearly labeled as AI-generated.
They must not be published on the internet at all.

questions.prompt: In the AI Value Chain, who is considered the "deployer"?

questions.prompt: To satisfy the OECD principle of "accountability," AI actors should ensure "traceability" throughout the system's lifecycle. What does this specifically help achieve?

Utilizing grammatically disparate structures to answer identical prompts.
Providing semantically disparate answers to semantically equivalent prompts.

Accuracy does not correlate with consistency.
Accuracy strictly correlates with consistency.
Accuracy conditionally correlates with consistency.
questions.solution: Research Overview: SaGE- Quantifying moral consistency in LLMs [22:45-23:58]: The SaGE study demonstrated that a model's benchmark accuracy does not correlate with its consistency at all.

questions.prompt: What does a ‘guarded’ attribute mean in a language model’s representation space?
options: The attribute can only be classified by specific linear probes.
The attribute requires non-linear transformations to be classified.

questions.prompt: What is the primary objective of modifying vectors from one distribution (e.g., toxic to non-toxic) to look like another?
options: To increase the computational cost of generating toxic content.

To fundamentally alter the underlying vocabulary of the model.
